questions.q: What are the four parts of the strong technical interview answer structure, in order?
options: Clarify scope, state the design decision, justify it, name a tradeoff
List every tool used, describe your job title, state your salary, thank the interviewer
Justify the decision, then state it, then clarify scope, then avoid tradeoffs
Name a tradeoff first, then explain why it doesn't matter
questions.explain: This order lets the interviewer follow your reasoning instead of having to reconstruct it — confirm the question, name the choice, explain why, then show you understand what you gave up.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say clarifying scope at the start of an answer isn't stalling?
options: It confirms what's actually being asked so the rest of the answer targets the real question instead of a guess
It gives the candidate extra time to think of an answer
Interviewers always expect at least thirty seconds of small talk first
It is only useful when the candidate doesn't know the answer
questions.explain: Without clarifying scope, a candidate risks answering a question the interviewer didn't actually ask, or going too deep or too shallow relative to what's wanted.

questions.q: In the worked example, why did the answer choose SSIS over Power Query for the work order ETL?
options: Because it needed to run as a repeatable, scheduled, standalone production pipeline rather than a transformation tied to one report
Because Power Query cannot read data from AdventureWorks under any circumstances
Because SSIS is always the faster tool to build with, regardless of the situation
Because the interviewer specifically required SSIS to be used
questions.explain: The justification step ties the tool choice to the actual requirement — a schedulable, standalone pipeline — rather than just naming the tool.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes skipping the "name a tradeoff" step a bigger red flag than picking an imperfect design in the first place?
options: It suggests the candidate has never questioned their own decision, which experienced interviewers notice more than an imperfect choice
It is a violation of most companies' interview policies
It means the candidate is lying about their experience
There is no real downside to skipping this step
questions.explain: Naming a real tradeoff shows self-awareness about the decision. Never naming one reads as either inexperience or a lack of critical thinking about your own work.

questions.q: If a practiced answer runs longer than about two minutes, what does this lesson recommend cutting first?
options: Detail from the justification step, while keeping scope, the decision itself, and the tradeoff intact
The entire tradeoff, since it's the least important part
The scope-clarifying question, since it isn't really part of the answer
The name of the tool used, to keep the answer more general
questions.explain: Scope, the decision, and the tradeoff are what an interviewer remembers — the justification step can be trimmed without losing the structure an interviewer is evaluating.
